Find the deepest density valley between two modes

Source: R/thresholds.R
density_valley.Rd

WHAT: smooths a histogram, locates peaks above peak_frac of the maximum, and returns the valley between the peak pair maximising depth * min(height). Returns NA when the distribution is unimodal – the honest answer, which then routes threshold resolution to the unstained-control fallback. WHY: for a bimodal marker the valley is the least-arbitrary cutoff available and adapts to each sample's own staining intensity.

Usage

density_valley(
  x,
  bins = 220L,
  smooth = 4,
  peak_frac = 0.02,
  min_gap_frac = 0.06,
  range_q = c(0.001, 0.999),
  min_rel_depth = 0.3,
  min_upper_frac = 0.002,
  floor = -Inf,
  prefer = c("deepest", "lowest"),
  min_lower_frac = 0.01,
  details = FALSE,
  noise_alpha = 0.05,
  ceiling = Inf
)

Arguments

x

A vector of values.

bins

The bins. Default 220L.

smooth

The smooth. Default 4.

peak_frac

The peak frac. Default 0.02.

min_gap_frac

The min gap frac. Default 0.06.

range_q

The range q. Default c(0.001, 0.999).

min_rel_depth

minimum valley depth AS A FRACTION of the smaller of the two flanking peaks. This is the parameter that makes minority positive populations findable – see the note on scoring below.

min_upper_frac

the upper mode must hold at least this fraction of events, so a cut cannot be placed out in the extreme tail where a handful of events form a bump.

floor

no cut is accepted at or below this value. Callers pass the transformed value of zero signal, transform$fn(0, marker): a stained population cannot sit below zero. Without it, the small bump that compensated events form below zero, next to the negative peak, scores as a deep separation, and the cut lands under the negative peak, so every cell is called positive. On one cohort that put 87% of CD45+ cells "Vd1+" and emptied every population defined as Vd1-. Default -Inf, no floor.

prefer

which qualifying valley to return. "deepest", the default, takes the best-separated pair of modes. "lowest" takes the qualifying valley nearest the bottom of the scale, which is what a gate meant to remove only NEGATIVE events needs: in whole blood the CD45 distribution has a negative mode, a dim mode (granulocytes) and a bright one (lymphocytes), the dim/bright valley is often the deepest, and taking it removed the granulocytes from the CD45+ parent. Used for the CD45 gate. Under "lowest" a valley also needs min_lower_frac of the events below it, so a ripple in the tail of the negative mode does not count as a separation.

min_lower_frac

see prefer. Default 0.01.

details

when TRUE return a list carrying the cut plus the relative depth of the valley and why no cut was found, instead of the bare cut. The default returns exactly what it always has: one number or NA_real_. threshold_uncertainty() uses the list form, because how deep a valley is determines how far the cut can move under resampling, and recomputing the smoothed histogram elsewhere would let the two drift apart.

noise_alpha

the family-wise rate at which counting noise alone may pass for a slope. A valley counts only where the density falls significantly from the first peak to it and rises significantly from it to the second, each judged against Poisson noise with a two-sided Bonferroni quantile over the non-overlapping smoothing windows (a SiZer-style test, Chaudhuri and Marron 1999). Relative depth alone does not see sample size: on single modes of 3,000 simulated events it found a valley in 81 of 150 samples, most of them below 95% of the events, and on a flat shoulder of a few events per bin it split the shoulder. Default 0.05; NA turns the test off.

ceiling

no cut is accepted at or above this value. Default Inf; the viability step passes the dye's dominant mode to look for a minimum below it (see apply_gate_hierarchy()).
